justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, anchored to what appears to be a baseline price level around 279–282. At the one-day horizon, I expected very little movement from the prevailing price, with the slight positioning toward 279.5 reflecting normal mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any immediate known catalysts. For the one-week estimate of 280.5, I incorporated a small positive drift consistent with a slight bullish bias in the underlying trend, while acknowledging that intraweek noise could easily overwhelm that signal. The one-month estimate of 282 represents a continuation of that gentle drift, essentially extrapolating a modest trend without expecting any dramatic regime change.

The confidence interval widths were primarily driven by realized and implied volatility at each horizon, scaled appropriately to the time elapsed. At one day, the 15-point range reflects typical daily fluctuation expectations. At one week, the range expands to roughly 27 points, consistent with weekly volatility that compounds daily uncertainty. At one month, the 54-point range reflects the much wider distribution of plausible outcomes as macroeconomic data, earnings, and sentiment shifts have more time to accumulate. I also weighted the intervals slightly asymmetrically in places to account for the possibility that downside moves can be sharper and faster than upside moves, particularly in risk-off environments.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharp inflation reading, a Fed policy shift, or a sudden credit event — could easily push prices well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. Geopolitical escalation or a liquidity shock could amplify selling pressure beyond normal distributional assumptions. On the upside, an unexpected dovish pivot, strong earnings surprises, or a short-squeeze dynamic could propel prices above 309. The intervals are calibrated to 90% confidence, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes should fall outside them under normal conditions, but fat-tail events in financial markets occur more frequently than standard models predict, so I would treat the outer bounds with appropriate humility.
